source_refs.note: Exercise 11.2, Question 3 (book page 211): solve graphically, parts (i)-(ii). The answer key (PDF 309) prints no answer for Q3; answers x = pi/4 and x = 0 are ours, checked. Solution book PDF 1019-1020.

blocks.explanation:
Solve an equation by drawing: the solution is where the two curves cross.
Plan: table of \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) on \([0, \pi]\), draw both, read the crossing point, check it.
steps:
Given: \(\sin x = \cos x\), \(x \in [0, \pi]\).
To find: the value(s) of \(x\) in \([0, \pi]\).
Method: to solve \(f(x) = g(x)\) graphically, draw \(y = f(x)\) and \(y = g(x)\) on the same axes; the x-coordinates of their points of intersection are the solutions.

Table of values (shown below the answer)
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}:\ \sin x = 0.5,\ \cos x \approx 0.87\]
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}:\ \sin x \approx 0.71,\ \cos x \approx 0.71\]
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}:\ \sin x \approx 0.87,\ \cos x = 0.5\]
Why: standard angles give exact values; at \(\pi/4\) the two rows become equal.

Draw both curves
\(y = \sin x\) rises from \((0, 0)\) to \((\pi/2, 1)\) and falls back to \((\pi, 0)\). \(y = \cos x\) falls from \((0, 1)\) through \((\pi/2, 0)\) to \((\pi, -1)\).
Why: one curve rises while the other falls on the first part, so they can cross only once there.

Read the intersection
\[\text{Point of intersection} \approx \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\ 0.71\right)\]
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\]
Why: before \(\pi/4\) cosine is above sine, after it sine is above. For \(x \in (\pi/2, \pi]\), \(\sin x \ge 0 > \cos x\), so there is no second crossing.

Check
\[\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\]
Why: both sides are equal at \(x = \pi/4\) (\(45^{\circ}\)).

answer_figure.alt: y = sin x and y = cos x from 0 to pi: the rising sine curve and the falling cosine curve cross once, at (pi/4, 0.71).
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (i): y = sin x and y = cos x meet at x = π/4 (original drawing)

blocks.explanation:
One side is a curve (\(y = \sin x\)), the other a straight line (\(y = x\)); the solution is where they meet.
Plan: measure \(x\) in radians (plain numbers), use the same scale on both axes, draw both, read the meeting point.
steps:
Given: \(\sin x = x\), \(x \in [0, \pi]\).
To find: the value(s) of \(x\) in \([0, \pi]\).
Method: to solve \(f(x) = g(x)\) graphically, draw \(y = f(x)\) and \(y = g(x)\) on the same axes; the x-coordinates of their points of intersection are the solutions.
Here \(x\) must be in radians, because it is compared with the number \(\sin x\).

Table of values (calculator in radian mode)
\[x = 0.5:\ \sin x \approx 0.48\]
\[x = 1:\ \sin x \approx 0.84\]
\[x = 2:\ \sin x \approx 0.91\]
Why: these are not standard angles, so the calculator gives the values; the line \(y = x\) simply has \(y\) equal to \(x\).

Draw both graphs
Use the same scale on both axes. \(y = \sin x\) rises from \((0, 0)\) to about \((1.57, 1)\) and falls to \((\pi, 0)\). \(y = x\) is the straight line through the origin at \(45^{\circ}\).
Why: with equal scales the line \(y = x\) makes a true \(45^{\circ}\) angle and the comparison is fair.

Read the intersection
\[\text{The graphs meet only at } (0,\ 0)\]
\[x = 0\]
Why: in the table \(\sin x\) is always smaller than \(x\) for \(x > 0\) (\(0.48 < 0.5\), \(0.84 < 1\), ...). For \(x > 1\), \(\sin x \le 1 < x\). Near 0 the curve touches the line at the origin and then stays below it.

Check
\[\sin 0 = 0\]
\[x = 0.5:\ 0.5 - \sin 0.5 \approx 0.02 > 0\]
Why: \(x = 0\) satisfies the equation, and even very close to 0 the line is already above the curve, so there is no other meeting point.

answer_figure.alt: y = sin x and the line y = x from 0 to pi with the same scale on both axes: the line stays above the sine curve and they meet only at the origin.
answer_figure.caption: Question 3 (ii): y = sin x and y = x meet only at (0, 0) (original drawing)
